column5: Common: city, book | Proper: Dhaka, Monday
column6: Common nouns name general things and start lowercase. Proper nouns name specific people, places, days, or months and always begin with a capital letter.
column7: Always capitalize days, months, languages, and nationalities (English, Friday, January).
column8: I live in a big city.||Dhaka is the capital of Bangladesh.||My sister studies English every Monday.

column5: Countable: a book, two books | Uncountable: water, advice
column6: Countable nouns have singular and plural forms and can use a/an or numbers. Uncountable nouns represent substances or abstract ideas and take singular verbs.
column7: Never say 'an advice' or 'informations'; say 'a piece of advice' and 'some information'.
column8: She bought three apples at the market.||Can you give me some advice?||We need more information before deciding.

column5: +s / +es / -y→ies | Irregular: child→children
column6: Most nouns add -s or -es for plural. Nouns ending in consonant + y change to -ies. Irregular nouns change vowel or form completely.
column7: Remember people, children, men, women, teeth, feet, and mice never take -s.
column8: Two boxes arrived this morning.||The children are playing in the yard.||Many cities have busy train stations.

column5: Subject: I, you, he, she, it, we, they | Object: me, him, her, us, them
column6: Subject pronouns perform the action before the verb. Object pronouns receive the action after a verb or preposition.
column7: Use object pronouns after prepositions: 'between you and me', never 'between you and I'.
column8: She called him after the meeting.||We invited them to dinner tonight.||Please send the report to me.

column5: my/mine, your/yours, his/his, her/hers, our/ours, their/theirs
column6: Possessive adjectives come before a noun (my bag). Possessive pronouns stand alone without a noun (That bag is mine).
column7: Never write an apostrophe in its, hers, ours, yours, or theirs.
column8: This is my notebook and that one is yours.||Her house is near ours.||The cat licked its paws.

column5: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, themselves
column6: Use reflexive pronouns when the subject and object are the same person. Emphatic pronouns add stress to who did the action.
column7: By myself means alone; don't confuse 'each other' with 'themselves'.
column8: He taught himself to play guitar.||I fixed the bike myself.||Please help yourselves to some tea.

column5: Near: this (sg), these (pl) | Far: that (sg), those (pl)
column6: Demonstratives point to specific nouns by distance in space or time. Use this/these for nearby or current things and that/those for distant or past things.
column7: Match singular/plural with the verb: 'These shoes are new', not 'This shoes'.
column8: This coffee smells wonderful.||Those mountains look very tall.||These days people read on phones.

column5: a + consonant sound | an + vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u)
column6: Use a or an before singular countable nouns when mentioning something for the first time or talking about a job. Choose by pronunciation sound, not spelling.
column7: Say 'an hour' (silent h) and 'a university' (starts with /j/ sound).
column8: She is an engineer at a local firm.||Wait an hour before eating.||He attends a university in London.

column5: the + specific / unique / previously mentioned noun
column6: Use 'the' when both speaker and listener know which exact thing is meant, for unique objects (the sun), superlatives, rivers, and musical instruments.
column7: Do not use 'the' for general plural or uncountable nouns: 'Dogs are loyal', not 'The dogs are loyal'.
column8: Please close the door behind you.||The moon is bright tonight.||She plays the violin beautifully.

column5: No article + meals, sports, languages, general plurals
column6: Omit articles before general plural nouns, uncountable ideas, languages, meals, sports, and most country or city names.
column7: Say 'go to school / bed / work' without 'the' when talking about their main purpose.
column8: Breakfast is ready on the table.||Love conquers all difficulties.||They speak Bengali and English fluently.

column5: Affirmative: some | Negative & Questions: any
column6: Use 'some' in positive sentences and polite offers/requests. Use 'any' in negative statements and general questions.
column7: In polite offers use 'some': 'Would you like some water?' sounds warmer than 'any'.
column8: I have some fresh fruit in the kitchen.||Do you have any questions about the lesson?||There isn't any milk left.

column5: much + uncountable | many + countable plural | a lot of + both
column6: Use 'many' with countable plurals and 'much' with uncountable nouns, especially in questions and negatives. 'A lot of' works naturally in positive sentences for both.
column7: In positive statements prefer 'a lot of time' over 'much time'.
column8: How many books did you read this year?||We don't have much time left.||She has a lot of patience.

column4: Few, A Few, Little & A Little
column5: a few / a little = enough (positive) | few / little = almost none (negative)
column6: Use (a) few with countable nouns and (a) little with uncountable nouns. Adding 'a' gives a positive meaning; omitting 'a' emphasizes scarcity.
column7: Compare 'a few friends' (some, happy) vs 'few friends' (almost none, lonely).
column8: I have a few good ideas to share.||Few people knew the hidden shortcut.||There is a little sugar in the jar.

column5: both (2) + plural | either/neither + singular noun
column6: Use both, either, and neither when referring to exactly two items. 'Both' takes a plural verb; 'neither' and 'either' take singular verbs in formal English.
column7: Pair them accurately: both...and, either...or, neither...nor.
column8: Both options look reasonable to me.||Neither answer is completely right.||You can choose either tea or coffee.

column5: each = individual focus (2+) | every = group as a whole (3+)
column6: Both take singular nouns and singular verbs. 'Each' focuses on items one by one (and works with 'of'); 'every' treats all items together as a series.
column7: You can say 'each of the students', never 'every of the students' (use 'every one of').
column8: Each student received a personal certificate.||Every morning I walk for thirty minutes.||Each of the rooms has a balcony.

column5: some- (pos) | any- (neg/q) | no- (neg verb pos) | every- (all)
column6: Compound pronouns refer to unspecified people, things, or places. They ALWAYS take a singular verb even when the meaning feels plural.
column7: Never use a double negative: say 'Nobody came', not 'Nobody didn't come'.
column8: Everyone is excited for the festival.||Did anyone leave an umbrella here?||Nothing seems impossible with daily practice.

column5: all + plural/uncountable | the whole + singular countable
column6: 'Whole' goes after determiners (the whole day) with singular countable nouns. 'All' goes before determiners (all the day / all students).
column7: Say 'the whole world' rather than 'whole the world'.
column8: She read the whole novel in two days.||All students must submit their essays.||Most people enjoy listening to music.

column5: People/animals: Maya's bag | Things/abstract: the roof of the house
column6: Use 's for people, animals, organizations, and time expressions (today's news). Use 'of' mainly for inanimate objects and formal phrases.
column7: For plural nouns ending in -s add only an apostrophe: 'the teachers' lounge'.
column8: Today's lesson covers articles and nouns.||My parents' house is by the river.||The color of the sky changed quickly.

column5: team / family / staff + singular (unit) or plural (individuals)
column6: Collective nouns name groups (committee, audience, staff). Use a singular verb when the group acts as one unit; British English allows plural when members act individually.
column7: Be consistent within the same sentence: 'The team won its match', not 'their match' after singular 'was'.
column8: The committee has approved the new plan.||My family lives near the coast.||The audience was silent during the solo.

column5: noun + noun (first noun acts like adjective, usually singular)
column6: In compound nouns the first noun describes the second and stays singular (a toothbrush, a five-star hotel). Hyphenate number + noun modifiers before a noun.
column7: Say 'a ten-minute walk', never 'a ten-minutes walk'.
column8: We took a fifteen-minute break at noon.||She bought a pair of running shoes.||He works in a high-speed train station.

column5: Subject + V1 (+ s/es for he/she/it)
column6: Describes permanent truths, daily habits, routines, and fixed timetables. Add -s/-es for third-person singular subjects in affirmative statements.
column7: Drop -s after does/doesn't: 'Does she work here?', never 'Does she works?'.
column8: Water freezes at zero degrees Celsius.||He reads the newspaper every morning.||The bus leaves at seven thirty.

column5: Subject + am/is/are + V-ing
column6: Expresses actions happening right now, temporary situations around the present, changing trends, and confirmed personal arrangements in the near future.
column7: Avoid continuous with stative verbs like know, believe, want, or own.
column8: They are studying for tomorrow's exam.||Prices are rising steadily this year.||I am meeting my mentor after lunch.

column5: Routine (I work) vs Temporary/Now (I am working)
column6: Use Present Simple for permanent states and repeated routines; use Present Continuous for temporary activities happening now or around now.
column7: 'I live in Dhaka' (permanent) vs 'I am living in Dhaka this month' (temporary).
column8: She usually drives, but today she is taking the train.||He speaks three languages fluently.||Quiet please, the baby is sleeping.

column5: Stative: know, love, seem, belong (normally Simple)
column6: Stative verbs describe thoughts, feelings, senses, and possession rather than physical action. Some verbs (think, have, taste) change meaning when used continuously.
column7: 'I think it's great' (opinion) vs 'I'm thinking about moving' (mental process).
column8: I believe your story completely.||This soup tastes delicious!||She is having lunch with her team right now.

column5: Subject + V2 | Neg/Q: did not / Did + V1
column6: Describes actions that started and finished at a specific time in the past (yesterday, in 2020, last night). Main tense for storytelling.
column7: After did/didn't ALWAYS use V1 base form: 'I didn't see him', never 'I didn't saw'.
column8: We visited Cox's Bazar last winter.||Did you finish the assignment on time?||She wrote a brilliant letter yesterday.

column5: Subject + was/were + V-ing
column6: Shows an action in progress at a specific past moment or a background activity interrupted by a shorter Past Simple event.
column7: Pair 'while + Past Continuous' with 'when + Past Simple'.
column8: I was cooking dinner when the lights went out.||At 9 PM last night, they were watching a film.||While he was walking, it began to rain.

column5: Subject + have/has + V3
column6: Connects the past to the present: life experiences (ever/never), recent events with present results (just/already/yet), and states continuing from past to now (for/since).
column7: Never combine Present Perfect with finished past times like 'yesterday' or 'in 2018'.
column8: Have you ever traveled by ship?||She has just finished her presentation.||We have lived in this neighborhood since 2019.

column5: Unfinished time / result now (Perf) vs Finished time (Past)
column6: Choose Present Perfect when time is unspecified or still open (this week, today); choose Past Simple when a finished past time is stated or implied.
column7: 'I have lost my keys' (still lost) vs 'I lost my keys yesterday' (past fact).
column8: I have seen that documentary twice.||I saw that documentary last Friday.||She has worked here for five years.

column5: Subject + have/has + been + V-ing
column6: Emphasizes the duration or ongoing effort of an activity that began in the past and continues now (or just stopped with visible evidence).
column7: Use Simple for completed counts ('read 3 books'), Continuous for duration ('reading for 3 hours').
column8: I have been waiting at the station for forty minutes.||Her hands are dirty because she has been gardening.||How long have you been learning English?

column5: Subject + had + V3
column6: Clarifies which of two past actions happened first. The earlier event uses Past Perfect; the later event uses Past Simple.
column7: Avoid overusing had + V3 when events are already in chronological order with 'before/after'.
column8: The train had already left when we reached the platform.||She realized she had forgotten her wallet.||Before moving abroad, he had studied French.

column5: Subject + had + been + V-ing
column6: Focuses on how long an activity had been continuing right up to another past event or explains the cause of a past state.
column7: Focuses on process/duration before a past point, not just completion.
column8: They had been driving for six hours before stopping.||The streets were flooded because it had been raining all night.||She had been teaching for a decade before retiring.

column5: Subject + will + V1 | Neg: won't + V1
column6: Used for instant decisions made while speaking, promises, offers, refusals, and opinion-based predictions (I think, probably).
column7: Never use 'will' in time clauses after when, before, as soon as, or until: use Present Simple.
column8: I'll help you carry those heavy bags.||I think tomorrow will be sunny.||Call me as soon as you arrive.

column4: Be Going To for Plans & Evidence
column5: Subject + am/is/are + going to + V1
column6: Expresses intentions decided before speaking and predictions supported by visible present evidence (dark clouds, slipping).
column7: Use 'going to' for prior plans; use 'will' for spontaneous decisions.
column8: We are going to launch our website next month.||Look at those dark clouds — it's going to pour!||Are you going to attend the workshop?

column5: Subject + will be + V-ing
column6: Describes an action that will be in progress at a specific moment in the future, or politely asks about someone's plans.
column7: Very natural for polite questions: 'Will you be using the printer?' sounds softer.
column8: This time tomorrow I will be flying over the ocean.||Don't call at 8 PM; we'll be having dinner.||Will you be joining us for the hike?

column5: Subject + will have + V3
column6: Projects forward to a future deadline and states that an action will already be completed before that point (by Friday, by 2030).
column7: Almost always paired with 'by' or 'by the time + Present Simple'.
column8: By next June, she will have graduated from university.||We will have completed the bridge by December.||Will you have finished the report before noon?

column5: Subject + will have been + V-ing
column6: Measures how long an ongoing action will have lasted by a specific point in the future.
column7: Always combines a future reference point (by May) with a duration (for 5 years).
column8: By October, I will have been working here for ten years.||At midnight, they will have been traveling for twelve hours.||Next spring she will have been playing piano for six years.

column5: Present Simple = Timetables | Present Continuous = Personal plans
column6: Fixed public schedules (trains, flights, classes) use Present Simple. Personal arrangements with a set time/place use Present Continuous.
column7: 'The flight departs at 6 AM' (schedule) vs 'I'm flying to Tokyo tomorrow' (personal plan).
column8: The museum opens at nine tomorrow.||We are having dinner with Sarah on Friday.||My exam starts at two o'clock.

column4: Future in the Past (Was Going To / Would)
column5: was/were going to + V1 | would + V1
column6: Used when looking forward from a point in the past—to express unfulfilled plans (was going to) or past predictions (knew it would).
column7: 'I was going to call you' usually implies you didn't end up calling.
column8: I was going to text you, but my battery died.||She knew the project would succeed.||They were about to leave when the bell rang.

column5: be + V-ing/V3 | have + V3 | do + V1 (Q/Neg)
column6: Primary auxiliaries build continuous, passive, perfect, question, and negative structures without carrying main dictionary meaning.
column7: Remember 'do' can also be a main verb: 'What do you do?' (first is auxiliary, second is main verb).
column8: Do you enjoy reading mystery novels?||She has never missed a single deadline.||The room was cleaned before guests arrived.

column5: Subject + can/could + V1 (bare infinitive)
column6: 'Can' expresses present ability and informal requests. 'Could' expresses past general ability and polite requests.
column7: Never add 'to' or -s after modals: say 'He can swim', not 'He cans to swim'.
column8: She can speak four languages fluently.||Could you pass me the salt, please?||When I was five, I could already ride a bike.

column5: could = general past ability | was able to = single past achievement
column6: For general skills in the past, use 'could'. When describing successfully managing one difficult specific event, use 'was/were able to' or 'managed to'.
column7: Say 'We were able to escape the fire', NOT 'We could escape the fire' (in negative 'couldn't' works for both).
column8: He could run very fast as a teenager.||Despite the traffic, I was able to catch the flight.||She couldn't find her glasses anywhere.

column5: Subject + may/might + V1
column6: Both express uncertain future or present possibility ('might' slightly less certain). 'May' also asks or grants formal permission.
column7: 'May not' means possibly not or prohibited; never contract 'may not' to 'mayn't'.
column8: It might rain later this afternoon.||May I borrow your dictionary for a minute?||She may join the conference online.

column5: must = internal/strong rule | have to = external rule
column6: Both express necessity in the affirmative. 'Must' often reflects the speaker's personal feeling or official notices; 'have to' reflects outside rules and works in past/future.
column7: In the negative their meanings split sharply: 'mustn't' = forbidden, 'don't have to' = not necessary!
column8: I must remember to call my mother today.||Students have to wear ID cards on campus.||You don't have to pay; entry is free.

column5: mustn't = prohibition | don't have to = no obligation
column6: 'Mustn't' warns that something is forbidden or dangerous. 'Don't have to' means you have a choice because it is optional.
column7: Learners often say 'You mustn't come' when they mean 'You don't have to come'—be careful!
column8: You mustn't touch those live wires.||You don't have to wear a tie on Fridays.||Visitors mustn't feed the wild animals.

column5: Subject + should / ought to + V1
column6: Give friendly advice, recommendations, or express what is expected/probable. 'Should' is far more common in questions and everyday speech.
column7: Use 'should + V1' without 'to', but 'ought + to + V1'.
column8: You should get at least seven hours of sleep.||We ought to leave early to beat traffic.||The package should arrive by Thursday.

column5: Subject + had better ('d better) + V1
column6: Gives strong advice for a specific immediate situation, implying a negative consequence if ignored.
column7: Never add 'to': say 'You'd better hurry', not 'You'd better to hurry'. Negative is 'had better not'.
column8: You'd better take an umbrella before the storm hits.||We had better not miss the last ferry.||He'd better apologize before things get worse.

column5: Would you like...? | When young, we would + V1
column6: Use 'would' for polite invitations/requests, hypothetical situations, and nostalgic repeated past actions (never past states).
column7: Use 'used to' (not 'would') for past states like 'I used to live in Sylhet'.
column8: Would you mind lowering the volume?||Every summer we would swim in the pond.||I would love a cup of green tea.

column4: Used To vs Be Used To vs Get Used To
column5: used to + V1 (past habit) | be/get used to + V-ing/noun (accustomed)
column6: 'Used to + V1' describes a past habit that stopped. 'Be used to + V-ing' means familiar with; 'get used to + V-ing' means becoming familiar with.
column7: After 'be/get used to', 'to' is a preposition so it takes -ing: 'I am used to waking early'.
column8: I used to bite my nails as a child.||She is used to working night shifts.||You will soon get used to the humid weather.

column5: must be (95% sure) | might/could be (possible) | can't be (impossible)
column6: Express logical certainty about present situations based on evidence. Never use 'mustn't be' for logical impossibility—always use 'can't be'.
column7: Opposite of 'He must be tired' is 'He can't be tired', never 'He mustn't be tired'.
column8: Her lights are on, so she must be home.||That can't be true — he was with me all day!||He isn't answering; he might be in a meeting.

column5: must/might/can't + have + V3
column6: Make logical guesses about past events from current evidence. 'Must have' = almost certain it happened; 'can't/couldn't have' = almost certain it didn't.
column7: Pronounce 'have' weakly (/əv/), never write 'must of'.
column8: The ground is wet; it must have rained overnight.||She can't have forgotten—I reminded her twice.||They might have taken the earlier train.

column4: Should Have / Could Have / Would Have
column5: should/could/would + have + V3
column6: Express past regret, criticism, missed opportunities, or unreal past results.
column7: 'Should have done' = it was wise to do it, but you didn't.
column8: I should have studied harder for the interview.||You could have told me you were coming!||I would have helped, but nobody asked me.

column4: Needn't Have vs Didn't Need To
column5: needn't have + V3 (did it unnecessarily) | didn't need to (didn't do it)
column6: 'Needn't have' means an action was done, but turned out unnecessary. 'Didn't need to' usually means we knew it wasn't required, so we skipped it.
column7: Great B2/IELTS distinction for precise storytelling.
column8: You needn't have brought food — we already ordered plenty!||I didn't need to cook because we ate out.||She needn't have worried; the test was easy.

column5: Shall I/we + V1? | Formal legal: shall + V1
column6: In modern English, 'shall' is chiefly used in polite offers/suggestions with I/we ('Shall we begin?') and formal contracts/rules.
column7: Do not use 'shall' with he/she/they in everyday conversation.
column8: Shall I open the window for some fresh air?||Shall we meet at the café at five?||All applicants shall submit original transcripts.

column4: Be Supposed To & Be Bound To
column5: be supposed to + V1 (expected) | be bound to + V1 (certain)
column6: 'Be supposed to' states rules, expectations, or plans that may not happen. 'Be bound to' expresses strong certainty that something will occur.
column7: 'Was supposed to' often signals a broken plan: 'It was supposed to be sunny!'
column8: We are supposed to submit the draft by Friday.||With so much practice, you are bound to improve.||This movie is supposed to be hilarious.

column5: be allowed to + V1 | How dare you...!
column6: 'Be allowed to' supplies past and future forms for permission ('was allowed to', 'will be allowed to'). 'Dare' expresses courage or indignation.
column7: Use 'was allowed to' instead of 'could' for specific past permission.
column8: Were you allowed to take photos inside the gallery?||Nobody dared to interrupt the keynote speaker.||How dare he blame the interns for his mistake!

column5: Subject + linking verb + Adjective (NOT Adverb)
column6: Linking verbs connect the subject to a state or quality rather than an action, so they take adjectives instead of adverbs.
column7: Say 'The flowers smell sweet' and 'I feel bad', not 'smell sweetly' or 'feel badly'.
column8: Your plan sounds practical and affordable.||She became confident after joining the debate club.||The sky grew dark before the thunderstorm.

column5: Transitive: needs object (raise) | Intransitive: no object (rise)
column6: Transitive verbs pass action to an object (She raised her hand). Intransitive verbs stand complete without an object (The sun rises) and cannot be made passive.
column7: Watch classic pairs: rise/raise, lie/lay, sit/set, arrive (no direct object).
column8: The sun rises early in summer.||Please raise your hand if you have a question.||The train arrived on time.

column5: The door opened (intrans) | He opened the door (trans)
column6: Ergative verbs (open, break, melt, boil, grow, sink) let the affected object become the subject without needing passive voice.
column7: Natural English prefers 'The glass broke' when no agent is mentioned.
column8: The ice melted rapidly in the warm sun.||The shop closes at nine every evening.||Sales increased by twenty percent last quarter.

column5: am/is/are + V3 | was/were + V3 (+ by agent)
column6: Use passive voice when the action or receiver matters more than who performed it, or when the doer is unknown or obvious.
column7: Only transitive verbs can form passives; omit 'by someone' when unimportant.
column8: Coffee is grown in Brazil and Colombia.||The telephone was invented in 1876.||These bags are handmade by local artisans.

column5: am/is/are being + V3 | was/were being + V3
column6: Describes an ongoing action being done to the subject right now or at a moment in the past.
column7: Always include 'being' before V3: 'is being repaired', never 'is repaireding'.
column8: The bridge is being repaired this week.||My laptop was being updated when the power cut.||New trees are being planted along the avenue.

column5: have/has been + V3 | had been + V3 | will have been + V3
column6: Expresses completed actions affecting the subject without focusing on the agent. Essential in news reports and academic writing.
column7: Never drop 'been': 'has been sent', not 'has sent' (unless active).
column8: All invitations have already been sent.||The painting had been stolen before dawn.||The metro line will have been finished by next year.

column5: modal + be + V3 | modal + have been + V3
column6: Combine modals (can, must, should, might) with 'be + V3' for rules, possibilities, and advice focusing on the target.
column7: Great for formal signs and essays: 'Safety helmets must be worn'.
column8: This form must be signed before submission.||The error could have been avoided easily.||Plastic waste should be recycled properly.

column5: Subject + get + V3
column6: Informal spoken alternative to be-passive, commonly used for sudden, unexpected, or personal events (get hurt, get hired, get stuck, get married).
column7: Avoid get-passive with stative verbs like 'know' or 'own'.
column8: He got promoted after leading the project.||Our car got stuck in the mud.||Be careful not to get sunburned at the beach.

column5: have/get + object + V3 (arranged service)
column6: Use 'have/get something done' when you pay or arrange for a professional to do a task for you—or when something unfortunate happens to you.
column7: Compare 'I cut my hair' (myself) vs 'I had my hair cut' (at the barber).
column8: I need to have my car serviced this weekend.||She got her passport renewed in three days.||He had his bicycle stolen outside the library.

column5: make/let/have + person + V1 | get + person + to + V1
column6: 'Make' forces someone, 'let' gives permission, 'have' assigns a task, and 'get' persuades someone. Notice 'get' requires 'to + V1' while make/let/have take bare V1.
column7: In passive voice, 'make' regains 'to': 'He was made to wait'.
column8: The teacher made us rewrite the introduction.||My parents let me choose my own major.||I got my brother to help me paint the room.

column5: It is said that... | Subject + is believed to + V1
column6: Formal structure for news and academic writing to report general beliefs, rumors, or research without naming a source.
column7: For past events use perfect infinitive: 'He is believed to have fled'.
column8: It is widely believed that sleep improves memory.||The ancient temple is thought to be over 1,000 years old.||She is rumored to have resigned yesterday.

column5: He said (that) + tense shifted one step back
column6: When reporting what someone said in the past, shift pronouns, time words (today→that day), and verbs one tense back (present→past, will→would).
column7: No backshift is needed if the reporting verb is present ('She says...') or the fact is still universally true.
column8: Direct: "I am tired." → She said she was tired.||Direct: "I will call tomorrow." → He said he would call the next day.||She told me that she had finished the book.

column4: Say vs Tell in Reported Speech
column5: say (+ to person) + that | tell + person + that
column6: 'Tell' MUST be followed immediately by a personal object (told me, told Sarah). 'Say' does not take a personal object directly (use 'said to me' or just 'said that').
column7: Never write 'He told that...' or 'He said me...'.
column8: She told me that the exam was postponed.||He said that he loved the new design.||Could you tell us the exact address?

column5: asked + if/whether / wh-word + Subject + Verb (statement order)
column6: When reporting a question, drop do/does/did and use normal statement word order (Subject before Verb), with a period instead of a question mark.
column7: Say 'She asked where I lived', NEVER 'She asked where did I live?'.
column8: He asked if I could speak Japanese.||She asked where the nearest pharmacy was.||They wanted to know whether the flight was delayed.

column5: told / asked / advised + object + (not) to + V1
column6: Report imperatives and polite requests using an object + infinitive (to + V1). For negative commands put 'not' directly before 'to'.
column7: Always put 'not' before 'to': 'told me not to worry', never 'to not worry'.
column8: The doctor advised him to drink more water.||She asked me not to open the window.||The officer ordered the driver to stop immediately.

column5: verb + to V1 (offer) | verb + V-ing (admit) | verb + obj + to V1 (remind)
column6: Replace repetitive 'said/told' with vivid reporting verbs: promise/refuse + to V1; admit/deny/suggest + V-ing; warn/encourage/remind + person + to V1.
column7: 'Suggest' NEVER takes 'person + to V1': say 'She suggested going' or 'suggested that we go'.
column8: He apologized for arriving late to the seminar.||She suggested taking a short break.||They warned us not to swim near the rocks.

column4: Time & Place Shifts in Reported Speech
column5: now→then | today→that day | yesterday→the day before | here→there
column6: Adjust perspective words when reporting speech at a different time or location so the listener understands the original context accurately.
column7: If you report the speech on the same day in the same place, keep 'today' and 'here'.
column8: She said she had met him the previous week.||He promised to send the files the following morning.||They mentioned that they were staying there until Sunday.

column5: If + Present Simple, Present Simple
column6: Describes scientific facts, rules, and automatic results that are always true whenever the condition happens. 'If' can often be replaced by 'when'.
column7: Both clauses use Present Simple—do not use 'will'.
column8: If you heat ice, it melts.||If I drink coffee at night, I can't sleep.||Plants die if they don't get enough sunlight.

column5: If + Present Simple, will/can/may + V1
column6: Expresses real, likely situations in the future and their probable consequences. Use a comma when the if-clause comes first.
column7: Never put 'will' inside the if-clause: say 'If it rains', NOT 'If it will rain'.
column8: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay indoors.||You will pass the exam if you practice daily.||If she finishes early, she might join us.

column5: If + Past Simple, would/could/might + V1
column6: Imagines hypothetical, unlikely, or impossible situations in the present or future. Formal English uses 'were' for all subjects ('If I were you').
column7: Past Simple here shows unreality, NOT past time.
column8: If I won the lottery, I would build a library.||If I were you, I would accept that scholarship.||What would you do if you could fly?

column5: If + Past Perfect (had V3), would/could + have + V3
column6: Imagines a different past and how its past result would have changed—used for regret, relief, or historical speculation.
column7: Both halves refer to finished past events that cannot be changed.
column8: If I had left five minutes earlier, I would have caught the bus.||She wouldn't have failed if she had reviewed her notes.||If they had known, they could have warned us.

column5: Past→Present: If + had V3, would + V1 | General→Past: If + V2, would have V3
column6: Mixes time frames: either a past choice affecting your present life (Type 3+2), or a permanent trait affecting a past event (Type 2+3).
column7: Look closely at time clues like 'now' or 'today' in the result clause.
column8: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.||If she spoke Spanish, she would have got that job.||If we hadn't missed the flight, we'd be on the beach right now.

column4: Unless, Provided That & As Long As
column5: unless = if...not | provided that / as long as = only if
column6: Alternative conditional conjunctions add nuance. 'Unless' already carries a negative meaning, so follow it with a positive verb.
column7: Never write 'Unless you don't hurry'—say 'Unless you hurry'.
column8: We'll go hiking unless it storms.||You can borrow my camera as long as you're careful.||Provided that everyone agrees, we'll start at ten.

column5: in case = precaution before | if = action only after
column6: 'In case' explains a precaution taken beforehand to be ready for a possible problem. 'If' means you wait until the condition happens.
column7: 'Take an umbrella in case it rains' (carry it now) vs 'Open it if it rains' (wait for rain).
column8: I saved a backup copy in case the computer crashes.||Write down my number in case you get lost.||Call me if you need directions.

column5: wish / if only + Past Simple (or were)
column6: Expresses a desire for a present reality to be different. 'If only' adds stronger emotion or longing.
column7: Do not use 'wish + will' for yourself; say 'I wish I knew', not 'I wish I know'.
column8: I wish I had more free time to read.||If only we lived closer to the sea!||She wishes she were taller.

column5: wish / if only + Past Perfect (had + V3)
column6: Expresses regret about something that happened or didn't happen in the past.
column7: Equivalent in meaning to 'I regret doing/not doing...'.
column8: I wish I hadn't spent so much money on gadgets.||If only we had booked the tickets last week!||He wishes he had listened to his coach's advice.

column5: Subject + wish + other person/thing + would + V1
column6: Expresses annoyance about someone's irritating habit or something you want to change now. Never use 'I wish I would' (different subjects required).
column7: Use only when the subjects differ: 'I wish you would...' or 'I wish it would stop raining'.
column8: I wish the neighbors would turn down their music.||I wish it would stop raining so we can play.||She wishes he wouldn't interrupt while she speaks.

column5: Should you need... | Were I to... | Had I known...
column6: Formal English drops 'if' and inverts the auxiliary (should / were / had) before the subject. Very impressive in business emails and C1/IELTS essays.
column7: Never contract negatives in inversion: 'Had I not seen it', NOT 'Hadn't I seen it'.
column8: Should you have any questions, please email our office.||Were I in your position, I would negotiate carefully.||Had we known about the traffic, we would have left earlier.

column5: recommend / insist / demand / vital + that + Subject + base V1
column6: After verbs/adjectives of urgency or recommendation, formal English uses the bare base verb (no -s, no past tense, 'be' instead of is/are).
column7: Say 'It is essential that he be present', not 'that he is present' in formal writing.
column8: The committee recommended that she submit a revised draft.||It is vital that every passenger wear a seat belt.||The manager insisted that the report be finished today.

column5: It's high time + Past Simple | would rather + Subject + Past Simple
column6: Both take Past Simple to express present/future preference or urgency for another person. With the same subject, 'would rather' takes bare V1.
column7: 'I'd rather stay home' (same subject) vs 'I'd rather you stayed home' (different subject).
column8: It's high time we upgraded our old software.||I'd rather walk than wait for the crowded bus.||I'd rather you didn't mention this to anyone yet.

column4: Prepositions of Time: At, On, In
column5: at (clock/night) | on (days/dates) | in (months/years/seasons)
column6: 'At' pinpoints exact times (at 7 PM, at noon). 'On' covers specific days and dates (on Monday, on July 4th). 'In' covers longer periods (in 2026, in winter, in the morning).
column7: No preposition before last, next, this, or every: 'see you next Friday', not 'on next Friday'.
column8: The class begins at nine o'clock sharp.||Her birthday is on March 15th.||We always travel to the village in December.

column4: Prepositions of Place: At, On, In
column5: at (exact point) | on (surface) | in (enclosed 3D space)
column6: Use 'at' for specific points/addresses (at the bus stop), 'on' for surfaces/streets/floors (on the table, on the 2nd floor), and 'in' for enclosed areas/cities/countries.
column7: Say 'in the car/taxi' (enclosed) vs 'on the bus/train/plane' (public transit you can walk on).
column8: She is waiting at the main entrance.||Your keys are on the kitchen counter.||They live in a quiet town in northern Japan.

column5: into, out of, onto, off, across, through, along, towards, past
column6: Movement prepositions show direction from one point to another. 'Across' crosses a flat surface; 'through' goes inside a tunnel, forest, or crowd.
column7: Don't use 'to' before 'home': say 'go home', not 'go to home'.
column8: The dog jumped over the low fence.||We walked through the park and across the bridge.||She walked into the studio with a bright smile.

column5: for + length of time | since + starting point | during + noun event
column6: 'For' measures duration (for two hours). 'Since' marks the start point (since 2021). 'During' tells when something happens inside a named period (during the lecture).
column7: Never use 'during' + a full clause; use 'while' + Subject + Verb instead.
column8: I have studied English for three years.||He hasn't eaten anything since breakfast.||Please turn off your phone during the exam.

column5: by = deadline (at or before) | until = continuous up to a point
column6: Use 'by' for a single action completed on or before a deadline. Use 'until' for a state or ongoing activity continuing up to a stopping point.
column7: 'Finish by 5 PM' (deadline) vs 'Work until 5 PM' (continuous until 5).
column8: Please submit your application by Friday afternoon.||We stayed at the library until closing time.||By tomorrow morning, the storm will have passed.

column5: between = distinct separate items | among = inside a crowd/group
column6: Use 'between' when naming individual distinct items (even more than two: between Dhaka, Tokyo, and London). Use 'among' when surrounded by an indistinct group.
column7: 'Divide the cake between the two kids' vs 'popular among teenagers'.
column8: The pharmacy is between the bank and the bakery.||She felt comfortable among old friends.||Negotiations continue between the three nations.

column5: over/under = directly vertical or covering | above/below = higher/lower level
column6: 'Over' and 'under' often imply direct vertical position or contact/covering. 'Above' and 'below' compare levels on a scale (temperature, sea level, floor).
column7: Use 'over' with numbers meaning 'more than': 'over 200 lessons'.
column8: The airplane flew above the clouds.||She spread a warm blanket over the sleeping child.||Temperatures dropped below zero overnight.

column5: on time = punctual / exact schedule | in time = early enough before too late
column6: 'On time' means matching the planned schedule. 'In time' means arriving with spare moments before a deadline or disaster.
column7: Think: trains run 'on time'; ambulances arrive 'in time' to save lives.
column8: The bullet train always departs on time.||We reached the gate just in time for boarding.||Will you be home in time for dinner?

column4: At the End vs In the End
column5: at the end (of sth) = final point | in the end = finally / after all
column6: 'At the end' refers to the physical or chronological conclusion of a thing. 'In the end' summarizes the ultimate outcome after difficulties or debate.
column7: Never say 'in the end of the movie'—say 'at the end of the movie'.
column8: There is a helpful glossary at the end of the book.||We argued for an hour, but in the end we agreed.||At the end of the month, I review my goals.

column5: listen to, apologize for, depend on, worry about, belong to
column6: Many English verbs require one fixed preposition before their object. Learning verb + preposition chunks prevents translation errors.
column7: Never say 'discuss about' or 'explain me'—say 'discuss the topic' and 'explain to me'.
column8: Success depends on consistent daily effort.||She apologized for missing the rehearsal.||Please listen carefully to the instructions.

column5: consist of, suffer from, agree with, deal with, recover from
column6: Master high-frequency verb-preposition pairs used in essays and workplace communication.
column7: 'Agree with' a person, 'agree to' a proposal, 'agree on' a price or date.
column8: The course consists of twelve interactive modules.||He recovered quickly from the seasonal flu.||Our team deals with international clients daily.

column5: good at, interested in, afraid of, proud of, responsible for
column6: Adjectives pair with specific prepositions that must be memorized as chunks—and any verb following a preposition MUST be in -ing form!
column7: Say 'good at swimming', NEVER 'good in swim'.
column8: She is extremely good at solving logic puzzles.||I am deeply interested in learning languages.||Who is responsible for updating the schedule?

column5: Preposition (of, in, about, without, before, after) + V-ing
column6: Whenever a verb comes right after ANY preposition, it MUST take the -ing (gerund) form—never the bare infinitive.
column7: Even 'to' takes -ing when it's a preposition: 'look forward to meeting you'!
column8: Thank you for helping me move yesterday.||He left the room without saying a word.||I look forward to hearing from you soon.

column4: Despite vs In Spite Of vs Although
column5: despite / in spite of + Noun/V-ing | although + Subject + Verb
column6: All three express contrast. 'Despite' and 'in spite of' are prepositions (followed by noun/V-ing); 'although' is a conjunction (followed by a full clause).
column7: NEVER write 'despite of'! Say 'despite the rain' or 'in spite of the rain'.
column8: Despite the heavy rain, the match continued.||In spite of feeling tired, she finished the essay.||Although it rained heavily, we enjoyed our trip.

column4: Because Of vs Due To vs Owing To
column5: because + clause | because of / due to / owing to + noun phrase
column6: Use 'because' before a subject + verb. Use 'because of', 'due to', or 'owing to' before a noun phrase to state a cause formally.
column7: In strict formal style, use 'due to' after the verb 'be' ('The delay was due to fog').
column8: The flight was delayed because of dense fog.||His success is due to years of quiet discipline.||We canceled the picnic because the wind was too strong.

column5: like + noun/pronoun (similarity) | as + job/role or clause
column6: Use 'like' to compare similarity ('works like a machine'). Use 'as' to state an actual role ('works as a teacher') or before a subject + verb clause.
column7: 'He spoke as a leader' (he IS one) vs 'He spoke like a leader' (similar to one).
column8: She works as a software architect in Tokyo.||He runs like the wind on the track.||As I mentioned earlier, practice beats cramming.

column4: By vs With for Means & Tools
column5: by + method/transport/V-ing | with + physical tool/instrument
column6: Use 'by' for methods, transport (by train, by hand), and passive agents. Use 'with' for the concrete instrument or body part used.
column7: Say 'cut with a knife' and 'go on foot' (exception to 'by').
column8: You can improve fluency by reading aloud daily.||She sketched the portrait with a charcoal pencil.||We traveled across Europe by train.

column5: Opinion → Size → Age → Shape → Color → Origin → Material → Purpose
column6: When stacking multiple adjectives before a noun, English follows a fixed natural sequence from subjective opinion to objective material/purpose.
column7: Keep descriptions crisp: 2–3 adjectives max before a noun sounds most natural.
column8: She bought a lovely small antique wooden jewelry box.||He drives a sleek new red Japanese sports car.||They live in a charming old stone cottage.

column5: -ing = causes the feeling | -ed = experiences the feeling
column6: Use -ing adjectives to describe the source (an exciting movie) and -ed adjectives to describe how a person feels (an excited viewer).
column7: Saying 'I am boring' means you bore others; say 'I am bored' when you feel boredom!
column8: The grammar lecture was surprisingly interesting.||The students felt inspired after the workshop.||Running a marathon is exhausting, so I'm exhausted.

column5: 1-syllable: +er | 2-syllable -y: -ier | long: more + adj + than
column6: Compare two items using -er for short adjectives and 'more' for longer adjectives. Always pair with 'than' when naming the second item.
column7: Never double up: say 'easier', NEVER 'more easier'. Irregulars: good→better, bad→worse, far→farther.
column8: This route is shorter than the highway.||Learning with audio is more effective than silent reading.||Today's weather is much better than yesterday's.

column5: the + adj-est / the most + adj (+ in place / of group)
column6: Compare three or more items to highlight the highest degree. Always include 'the' before a superlative adjective.
column7: Use 'in' with places/groups ('the tallest in the class'), 'of' with plural time/items ('the best of all').
column8: Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.||That was the most helpful tutorial I have ever watched.||She is the fastest runner on the team.

column5: as + base adj/adv + as | not as/so + adj + as
column6: Show that two things are equal or unequal in degree using the base adjective without -er or more.
column7: You can modify with 'twice as big as' or 'almost as fast as'.
column8: Your pronunciation is as clear as a native speaker's.||This laptop isn't as heavy as my old one.||Please reply as soon as possible.

column5: The + comparative..., the + comparative...
column6: Shows a direct cause-and-effect relationship where one change continuously drives another.
column7: Keep both halves parallel and concise for memorable style.
column8: The more you practice speaking, the more confident you become.||The earlier we depart, the less traffic we'll face.||The harder the puzzle, the sweeter the victory.

column5: Adj + -ly (careful→carefully) | Irregular: fast, hard, late, well
column6: Adverbs of manner describe HOW an action happens and usually follow the verb or object. Remember 'good' is an adjective while 'well' is its adverb.
column7: 'Hardly' means almost not, NOT the adverb of hard: say 'work hard', not 'work hardly'.
column8: She explained the complex rule clearly.||He plays the piano extraordinarily well.||They worked hard to meet the launch date.

column5: always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never
column6: Place frequency adverbs BEFORE main verbs ('I always study') but AFTER the verb 'to be' ('She is always punctual') and after the first auxiliary ('I have never been').
column7: 'Never' already makes the clause negative—don't add 'not'.
column8: I usually review flashcards on the train.||He is rarely late for morning meetings.||We have often discussed this topic together.

column5: too + adj/adv | adj/adv + enough | enough + noun
column6: 'Too' means more than desirable (negative result). 'Enough' means sufficient—placed AFTER adjectives/adverbs but BEFORE nouns.
column7: Never say 'enough strong'; always say 'strong enough'.
column8: The soup is too hot to eat right now.||Is the room bright enough for reading?||We don't have enough chairs for all the guests.

column5: so + adj/adv + that | such + (a/an) + adj + noun + that
column6: Both intensify a quality to introduce a dramatic result. Use 'so' before bare adjectives/adverbs; use 'such' when a noun follows.
column7: With 'much/many/few/little' use 'so' even before a noun: 'so many books'.
column8: The speech was so moving that everyone applauded.||It was such a beautiful sunset that we stopped to watch.||She spoke so quickly that I missed two words.

column5: Gradable: very tired | Extreme: absolutely exhausted
column6: Gradable adjectives (cold, big, tired) pair with 'very/fairly/quite'. Extreme adjectives (freezing, huge, exhausted) already include 'very', so pair them with 'absolutely/completely/totally'.
column7: Never say 'very freezing' or 'very exhausted'—say 'absolutely freezing'!
column8: It is absolutely freezing outside today.||Her presentation was totally brilliant.||I'm a bit tired, not completely exhausted yet.

column5: still (continuing) | yet (neg/Q up to now) | already (sooner than expected)
column6: 'Still' goes mid-sentence for ongoing situations. 'Yet' goes at the end of questions and negatives. 'Already' shows completion earlier than expected.
column7: Use 'already' in questions to express surprise: 'Have you finished already?'
column8: She is still working on the final chapter.||Have you received the confirmation email yet?||He has already mastered all twelve tenses.

column5: fairly (mild) < quite/pretty (moderate) < rather (strong/unexpected)
column6: Modifiers of degree fine-tune your tone. 'Rather' often introduces a surprise or negative quality, or precedes a comparative ('rather better').
column7: 'Quite' + extreme adjective means 'completely': 'You're quite right!'
column8: The exercise was fairly simple for beginners.||It's getting rather late; we should head home.||That explanation is pretty clear now.

column5: Verb + Manner + Place + Time
column6: When stacking multiple adverbs at the end of a sentence, English prefers Manner → Place → Time order (or Place → Manner after verbs of movement like go/arrive).
column7: Time adverbs can also move to the very front for emphasis: 'Yesterday, she spoke clearly.'
column8: She sang beautifully at the concert last night.||They arrived at the airport early this morning.||He worked quietly in the library all afternoon.

column5: Subject + Verb + Object (+ Place + Time)
column6: English relies strictly on Subject-Verb-Object order to show who does what. Never separate a verb from its direct object with a time or manner adverb.
column7: Say 'I like coffee very much', NEVER 'I like very much coffee'.
column8: My brother builds mobile apps.||She reads science articles every evening.||We enjoyed the concert at the stadium yesterday.

column5: Clause 1, + for/and/nor/but/or/yet/so + Clause 2
column6: Join two complete independent clauses of equal weight using a comma + coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS).
column7: Never join two complete sentences with ONLY a comma (comma splice)—add a conjunction or semicolon.
column8: I wanted to go for a run, but it started raining.||She studied consistently, so she aced the test.||You can take the bus, or we can walk together.

column5: who (people) | which (things) | that (both) | whose (possession) | where (place)
column6: Identifies exactly which person or thing you mean—essential to the sentence's meaning, with NO commas. You may omit who/which/that when it is the object of the clause.
column7: Never repeat the pronoun inside the clause: say 'the book that I read', NOT 'that I read it'.
column8: The teacher who inspired me retired last year.||This is the app (that) I use every morning.||That's the café where we first met.

column5: Noun, + who/which/whose + extra info, + Verb
column6: Adds optional bonus information about an already-identified noun, ALWAYS set off by commas. Never use 'that' and never omit the relative pronoun here.
column7: Non-defining 'which' can refer to an entire preceding clause: 'He arrived early, which surprised us.'
column8: My sister, who lives in Toronto, is visiting next week.||Dhaka, which sits on the Buriganga River, is vibrant and historic.||He passed on his first try, which made everyone proud.

column5: Active: V-ing (the girl smiling) | Passive: V3 (the bridge built in 1990)
column6: Shorten relative clauses by removing who/which + be. Use present participle (-ing) for active meaning and past participle (V3) for passive meaning.
column7: Ensure the participle's implied subject matches the main clause subject to avoid dangling modifiers!
column8: Anyone wanting a ticket should register today.||The bridge built in 1998 connects both regions.||Exhausted by the climb, the hikers rested at the summit.

column5: Subject or Object = that/what/how/whether + Subject + Verb
column6: A full clause functioning as a single noun (subject, object, or complement). Use statement word order inside the noun clause.
column7: 'What' means 'the thing(s) that'—never add 'that' after 'what'.
column8: What she said changed my entire perspective.||I don't know whether the shop is open today.||That he recovered so quickly amazed the doctors.

column5: when, while, before, after, until, as soon as, once
column6: Connect two events in time. Remember: when referring to the future, the time clause uses Present Simple or Present Perfect, NEVER 'will'.
column7: Use 'once' or 'as soon as' to show immediate sequence.
column8: As soon as the bell rings, the exam begins.||Wait here until I have checked the timetable.||Once you learn the core patterns, grammar feels logical.

column5: Reason: because, since, as | Purpose: so that, in order to
column6: State why something happens (reason) or the intended goal (purpose). 'In order to + V1' works for the same subject; 'so that + Subject + can/could' works for any subject.
column7: Avoid 'for to': say 'I came to learn', not 'I came for to learn'.
column8: She spoke slowly so that beginners could follow easily.||Since it was raining, we moved the session indoors.||He wakes up at six in order to exercise before work.

column5: although, even though, whereas, while, even if
column6: Highlight unexpected contrasts or compare two opposing facts cleanly. 'Even though' expresses a real fact; 'even if' expresses an imaginary condition.
column7: Never pair 'although' with 'but' in the same sentence!
column8: Even though the exam was tough, she scored ninety percent.||I prefer tea, whereas my brother drinks coffee.||We will finish the climb even if it gets dark.

column5: It is/was + Focused Element + that/who + rest of clause
column6: Spotlights one specific piece of information (who, when, where, or why) for emphasis or correction.
column7: Great for clear persuasion in speaking and writing.
column8: It was Sarah who spotted the subtle error.||It is daily consistency that builds real fluency.||It wasn't until midnight that the train finally arrived.

column5: What + Subject + Verb + is/was + Focused Element
column6: Builds anticipation by placing the highlighted idea at the end of the sentence, starting with 'What...'.
column7: Very natural in presentations and IELTS Speaking Part 3.
column8: What I admire most about her is her calm focus.||What you need right now is a good night's sleep.||What happened was that the server lost power.

column5: Complement / Adverbial + Subject + Verb (or Inverted Verb + Subject)
column6: Move an adjective, object, or prepositional phrase to the very start of the sentence to create literary punch or contrast.
column7: After fronted place phrases with be/stand/lie, invert subject and verb: 'On the hill stood an old tower.'
column8: Strange as it may seem, the shortest proof was the best.||Never have I seen such dedication.||At the end of the lane stood a quiet bookshop.

column5: Main Noun, + explanatory noun phrase, + Verb
column6: Rename or clarify a noun directly beside it without writing a clunky extra sentence. Use commas for non-essential appositives.
column7: Keep appositives tight so the subject and verb stay clearly connected.
column8: My mentor, a retired linguist, reviewed my thesis.||Tokyo, the world's largest metropolis, runs with remarkable precision.||Her latest book, a guide to clear writing, topped the charts.

column4: There Is / There Are & Dummy It
column5: There + be + real subject | It + be + weather/time/distance/adj + to V1
column6: 'There' introduces the existence of something (verb agrees with the noun AFTER be). 'It' acts as an empty subject for weather, time, distance, and 'It is easy to...'.
column7: Say 'There are many reasons', NOT 'There is many reasons'.
column8: There are over two hundred lessons in this academy.||It takes twenty minutes to walk to the river.||It is rewarding to learn a new language.

column5: V-ing as noun (Swimming is fun | I enjoy reading)
column6: A gerund looks like a verb ending in -ing but behaves like a noun—it can be a sentence subject, object of specific verbs (enjoy, avoid, mind, finish, keep), or object of a preposition.
column7: As a subject, a gerund takes a singular verb: 'Reading books expands vocabulary.'
column8: Speaking aloud improves pronunciation rapidly.||She avoided making the same mistake twice.||Would you mind closing the curtains?

column5: decide/want/hope/plan/promise + to V1 | adj + to V1
column6: Many verbs expressing intention, desire, or decision are followed by 'to + V1'. Adjectives describing reactions (happy, difficult, ready) also take 'to + V1'.
column7: Negative infinitive puts 'not' before 'to': 'She decided not to go.'
column8: They decided to launch the project in April.||It is easy to remember words with vivid stories.||He promised not to reveal the surprise.

column4: Verbs Changing Meaning: Remember, Forget, Stop, Try
column5: remember/forget + V-ing (past memory) vs to V1 (future duty)
column6: Some verbs take BOTH forms with totally different meanings! 'Stop smoking' = quit; 'stop to smoke' = pause in order to smoke. 'Try V-ing' = experiment; 'try to V1' = attempt hard.
column7: Master these four verbs—they appear constantly in grammar exams!
column8: I remember meeting him in Dhaka years ago.||Please remember to lock the balcony door.||She stopped to buy coffee on her way to class.

column4: Regret, Go On & Mean (+ V-ing vs to V1)
column5: regret V-ing (past sorrow) vs regret to say (formal bad news)
column6: 'Go on V-ing' means continue the same activity; 'go on to V1' means move to a new stage. 'Mean V-ing' = involve; 'mean to V1' = intend.
column7: Formal letters love: 'We regret to inform you that...'
column8: I regret losing my temper during the debate.||After college, she went on to found a startup.||Taking this job means relocating to another city.

column5: ask / advise / allow / encourage / expect / remind + person + to V1
column6: Expresses influencing, guiding, or expecting another person to act. Note that 'allow/advise' without an object take V-ing ('They don't allow parking here').
column7: Compare 'They don't allow smoking' vs 'They don't allow visitors to smoke'.
column8: My coach encouraged me to enter the tournament.||Please remind him to bring his passport.||We expect the package to arrive before Friday.

column4: Verbs of Perception + V1 vs V-ing
column5: see / hear / watch / feel + object + V1 (whole action) or V-ing (in progress)
column6: Use bare V1 when you witnessed the entire action from start to finish; use V-ing when you caught part of an action already in progress.
column7: Never put 'to' after active see/hear/watch: 'I heard her sing', not 'to sing'.
column8: I watched the artist paint the entire mural.||We heard someone knocking softly at the gate.||Did you feel the floor vibrate just now?

column5: being V3 / to be V3 | having V3 / to have V3
column6: Use passive forms when the subject receives the action ('hate being interrupted'). Use perfect forms when the action happened BEFORE the main verb ('proud of having finished').
column7: Essential for concise B2–C1 academic and storytelling style.
column8: Nobody enjoys being kept waiting in the rain.||She hopes to be selected for the fellowship.||He denied having seen the confidential file.

column5: it's no use / it's worth / can't help / have difficulty + V-ing
column6: Several everyday fixed expressions always require a gerund (-ing), even when they end in 'to' (be used to, look forward to, object to).
column7: Say 'It's worth visiting', never 'It's worth to visit'.
column8: This grammar guide is definitely worth bookmarking.||I couldn't help laughing at his clever pun.||She had no difficulty understanding the accent.

column5: Aux/Be/Modal + Subject + Main Verb? → Yes, S + Aux.
column6: Form Yes/No questions by inverting the auxiliary (do/does/did/am/is/are/have/can/will) before the subject. Natural short answers repeat the auxiliary instead of just saying 'Yes.'
column7: Don't contract positive short answers: say 'Yes, I am', NEVER 'Yes, I'm'.
column8: Do you enjoy learning new words? — Yes, I do!||Has she visited Japan before? — No, she hasn't.||Can we finish before sunset? — Yes, we can.

column5: Object Q: Who did you call? | Subject Q: Who called you?
column6: Normal Wh-questions use auxiliary + subject + verb. When Who/What/Which IS the subject, do NOT add do/does/did—use normal statement verb order!
column7: 'Who broke the vase?' (subject—no 'did') vs 'What did he break?' (object—uses 'did').
column8: Where did you learn to cook so well?||Who painted this gorgeous portrait?||Which bus goes directly to the airport?

column5: Positive statement, negative tag? | Negative statement, positive tag?
column6: Add a short auxiliary + pronoun tag at the end to confirm information or invite agreement. Match the tense and auxiliary of the main clause.
column7: Special tags: 'I am right, aren't I?', 'Let's go, shall we?', 'Open the door, will you?'.
column8: You've visited Sylhet before, haven't you?||He doesn't eat seafood, does he?||Let's take a short coffee break, shall we?

column5: Could you tell me / Do you know + wh-word/if + Subject + Verb?
column6: Soften direct questions into polite requests. Once inside the embedded question, drop do/does/did and use normal statement order!
column7: Say 'Do you know what time it is?', NEVER 'Do you know what time is it?'.
column8: Could you tell me where the station is?||Do you happen to know if the library is open?||I was wondering whether you could review my email.

column4: So Do I / Neither Do I (Agreement)
column5: Positive: So + Aux + Subject | Negative: Neither/Nor + Aux + Subject
column6: Agree quickly with someone's statement by mirroring their auxiliary verb. Use 'So' for positive statements and 'Neither' for negative ones.
column7: Match the original auxiliary: 'I've been there.' → 'So have I!' (not 'So do I').
column8: I love fresh mango. — "So do I!"||"I can't swim very far." — "Neither can I."||"She was thrilled by the news." — "So were we!"

column5: Subject + do/does/did + base V1 (in positive statements)
column6: Insert stressed do/does/did into a positive statement or imperative to contradict a doubt, express warm insistence, or emphasize a contrast.
column7: Always keep the main verb in bare base form after emphatic did: 'He did tell me!'
column8: I do appreciate all the time you spent helping us.||She didn't call, but she did send a thoughtful note.||Do sit down and make yourself comfortable!

column5: Never / Rarely / Seldom / Not only / Little + Aux + Subject + Verb
column6: Placing a negative or restrictive adverbial at the very start of a sentence triggers question-like auxiliary inversion for formal, dramatic impact.
column7: Remember 'Not only + Aux + S + V, but also...'.
column8: Never have I encountered such warm hospitality.||Not only did she win the race, but she also broke the record.||Rarely do we get an opportunity like this.

column5: No sooner + had + S + V3 + than... | Hardly/Scarcely + had + S + V3 + when...
column6: Formal storytelling structures showing that a second event occurred immediately after the first. Pair 'no sooner' with 'than' and 'hardly/scarcely' with 'when'.
column7: Never mix them: don't write 'No sooner... when' or 'Hardly... than'.
column8: No sooner had we sat down than the power went out.||Hardly had she stepped outside when it began to pour.||Scarcely had the concert ended when fans rushed the stage.

column5: I moved to Tokyo. → "Did you?" / "You moved WHERE?"
column6: Short reply questions ('Did you?', 'Has she?', 'Isn't it?') show active listening and surprise in natural English conversation without literally asking for verification.
column7: Use positive reply to positive statement and negative reply to negative statement!
column8: I've just published my first novel. — "Have you? Congratulations!"||"He didn't like the soup." — "Didn't he? I thought it was great."||"We walked twenty kilometers." — "Did you really?"

column5: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so
column6: Connect grammatically equal words, phrases, or independent clauses. 'Yet' introduces a surprising contrast; 'nor' adds a second negative idea (with inversion).
column7: 'For' as a conjunction meaning 'because' is literary; use 'because' in everyday speech.
column8: She was exhausted, yet she kept smiling warmly.||He neither called nor answered my messages.||Bring a jacket, or you might catch a chill.

column5: both...and | either...or | neither...nor | not only...but also
column6: Correlative pairs link balanced elements. Keep the grammar structure identical after both halves (noun + noun, verb + verb, phrase + phrase).
column7: With 'either...or' and 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the CLOSER subject!
column8: Neither the manager nor the assistants were informed.||She is not only fluent in English but also skilled in design.||You can either submit online or hand it in at reception.

column5: Sentence 1. Furthermore / Moreover / In addition, Sentence 2.
column6: Link supporting arguments smoothly in paragraphs and essays. Always follow sentence-initial transition adverbs with a comma.
column7: Use 'besides' in speech/informal writing; prefer 'furthermore/moreover' in formal essays.
column8: The app works offline. Moreover, it includes audio pronunciation.||Regular walking improves stamina. In addition, it reduces stress.||I'm too tired to go out; besides, it's pouring rain.

column4: Contrast Connectors (However, Nevertheless, On the Other Hand)
column5: Clause 1; however, Clause 2. / Sentence 1. Nevertheless, Sentence 2.
column6: Signal a shift or counterbalance between two sentences. Unlike 'but', 'however' is a conjunctive adverb—use a period or semicolon before it, never just a comma!
column7: Avoid comma splice: write '...tired; however, I finished', NOT '...tired, however, I finished'.
column8: The task looked daunting; however, we finished ahead of schedule.||Online courses save commute time. On the other hand, they require self-discipline.||The weather was bleak. Nevertheless, our spirits stayed high.

column5: Cause. Therefore / Consequently / As a result, Effect.
column6: Show logical conclusions clearly in academic essays, business emails, and reports. Follow with a comma at the start of a clause.
column7: Vary your connectors instead of repeating 'so' in every paragraph.
column8: Demand rose sharply; consequently, prices increased.||She practiced daily for six months. Therefore, her fluency soared.||He missed the deadline; as a result, the launch shifted.

column5: for instance, namely, in other words, specifically, that is to say
column6: Introduce concrete examples or restate complex points in simpler words to boost essay clarity and cohesion.
column7: Use 'such as' before noun examples without a comma after it: 'languages such as Bengali and Japanese'.
column8: Several skills boost career growth, such as clear writing and public speaking.||Two factors matter most, namely accuracy and consistency.||He is ambidextrous; in other words, he writes well with both hands.

column5: In conclusion, To sum up, Overall, Ultimately, All in all
column6: Signal the closing synthesis of an essay, email, or presentation without introducing brand-new unrelated arguments.
column7: 'In conclusion' suits formal essays; 'All in all' fits friendly reviews and speaking.
column8: In conclusion, daily short practice outperforms occasional cramming.||Overall, the workshop exceeded everyone's expectations.||Ultimately, clear communication is about helping your listener.

column5: Singular subject → verb+s | Plural subject → base verb
column6: The verb must always match the true grammatical subject in number, ignoring words tucked inside prepositional phrases between them.
column7: Find the head noun before 'of/in/with': 'The box of chocolates IS empty.'
column8: The quality of these lessons is outstanding.||My neighbors travel to the mountains every autumn.||A list of irregular verbs sits on my desk.

column4: Agreement with Together With / As Well As
column5: Subject 1, as well as / along with Subject 2, + verb matching Subject 1
column6: Phrases like 'as well as', 'together with', 'along with', and 'including' do NOT make a singular subject plural—match the verb strictly to the first subject.
column7: Unlike 'and', 'along with' leaves a singular subject singular!
column8: The director, along with her engineers, is visiting today.||My sister, as well as her friends, loves hiking.||The book, including all appendices, weighs two kilograms.

column5: Five kilometers IS... | Ten dollars IS... | Two hours IS...
column6: Expressions of total money, time, distance, or weight treated as one single sum take a singular verb.
column7: Say 'Three hours is a long time to wait', not 'Three hours are'.
column8: Fifty dollars is a fair price for that jacket.||Ten kilometers is too far to walk in this heat.||Two weeks goes by quickly during vacation.

column4: A Number Of vs The Number Of
column5: A number of + plural noun + PLURAL verb | The number of + plural noun + SINGULAR verb
column6: 'A number of' means 'several/many' (plural verb). 'The number of' refers to the single statistical count itself (singular verb).
column7: Classic exam favorite: 'A number of students ARE...' vs 'The number of students IS...'.
column8: A number of learners have already completed the challenge.||The number of daily active users is rising rapidly.||A large number of books were donated to the school.

column5: news, physics, economics, luggage → Singular | trousers, scissors, glasses → Plural
column6: Some nouns end in -s yet are uncountable singular (news, mathematics, series). Paired tools/clothes (scissors, jeans, glasses) are always plural unless preceded by 'a pair of'.
column7: Never say 'a good news' or 'the news are'; say 'the news is'.
column8: The morning news is encouraging today.||Physics requires both intuition and careful math.||Where are my reading glasses? A new pair is on the desk.

column4: One Of The + Plural Noun + Who/That
column5: One of the students IS... | one of the students who ARE...
column6: 'One of the + plural noun' takes a singular verb because 'one' is the subject. Inside 'one of the [plural] who...', the relative clause usually takes a plural verb (unless 'the only one of...').
column7: Always use a PLURAL noun after 'one of the': 'one of the best books', NEVER 'one of the best book'.
column8: One of my favorite hobbies is photography.||She is one of the writers who inspire young readers.||He is the only one of the finalists who lives locally.

column5: Separable: turn off the light / turn it off | Inseparable: look after him
column6: With separable phrasal verbs, a noun object can go in the middle or at the end—but a PRONOUN object (it, them, him) MUST go in the middle!
column7: Say 'turn it off' and 'pick me up', NEVER 'turn off it' or 'pick up me'.
column8: Please turn off the lights — or turn them off before leaving.||She looks after her younger brother after school.||Could you fill out this form and hand it in?

column5: get up, get over, get along with, get through, get away with
column6: 'Get' combines with particles to cover daily routines, recovery, relationships, and success. Learn them in context sentences rather than dry lists.
column7: 'Get over' = recover from illness/heartbreak; 'get along' = have a friendly relationship.
column8: It took him two weeks to get over the flu.||Do you get along well with your new coworkers?||We finally got through all the practice questions.

column5: take off, take up, take over, take after, take in
column6: 'Take' phrasal verbs appear constantly in travel, hobbies, work, and family descriptions. Notice 'take off' has multiple meanings (flight departs, remove coat, become suddenly successful).
column7: 'Take up a hobby' = start doing it regularly.
column8: The airplane took off smoothly despite the wind.||She decided to take up calligraphy this winter.||He really takes after his grandfather in temperament.

column5: make up (invent/reconcile), make out (discern), do without, do over
column6: Learn common phrasal verbs plus classic make/do collocations (make a decision/mistake/progress vs do homework/business/a favor).
column7: Remember: we MAKE a mistake and DO our best.
column8: They argued yesterday, but they made up this morning.||I could barely make out the sign in the fog.||Could you do me a quick favor?

column5: put off (postpone), put up with (tolerate), give up (quit), give in (surrender)
column6: Essential verbs for expressing procrastination, endurance, persistence, and generosity.
column7: 'Put off' is followed by V-ing: 'Don't put off studying!'
column8: Never put off until tomorrow what you can do today.||She refused to give up even after three setbacks.||How do you put up with that loud construction noise?

column5: look up, look into, look forward to, come across, come up with
column6: Master these for research, problem-solving, and reading comprehension. Remember 'look forward to' takes V-ing!
column7: 'Come across' = find by chance; 'come up with' = invent an idea/solution.
column8: I came across a rare dictionary at the book fair.||The team came up with a brilliant solution.||We'll look into the issue right away.

column5: Verb + Adverb + Preposition (inseparable): run out of, catch up with, cut down on
column6: Three-word phrasal verbs are ALWAYS inseparable—place nouns and pronouns at the very end.
column7: High-scoring natural vocabulary for IELTS Speaking and daily fluency.
column8: We ran out of coffee beans this morning.||I need to catch up on my sleep this weekend.||The doctor advised him to cut down on refined sugar.

column4: High-Frequency Phrasal Verbs: TURN, SET & BRING
column5: turn down (reject), set up (establish), bring up (raise topic/child), bring about (cause)
column6: Widely used in business English, interviews, and journalism.
column7: 'Turn down an offer' = politely decline; 'turn up' = arrive unexpectedly.
column8: She turned down the job offer to pursue her own studio.||They set up a free community library in the town.||He brought up an important question during the meeting.

column5: First word, pronoun 'I', proper nouns, titles, languages, days/months
column6: Always capitalize the pronoun 'I', sentence starts, names of people, places, days, months, holidays, and languages—but NOT seasons (spring, winter) or school subjects (math, history) unless they are languages.
column7: Write 'English and physics', not 'english and Physics'.
column8: My friend Tariq speaks Bengali, English, and Japanese.||We plan to visit Kyoto next autumn.||Every Tuesday morning I practice speaking.

column4: Comma Rules: Lists, Intro Phrases & Clauses
column5: A, B, and C | Intro phrase, main clause | Clause 1, but Clause 2
column6: Use commas to separate items in a series, after introductory adverbs/clauses, around non-essential extra info, and before FANBOYS joining two full sentences.
column7: Never place a single comma directly between a subject and its verb!
column8: We packed notebooks, pens, chargers, and snacks.||After finishing dinner, we went for a brisk walk.||She wanted to stay longer, yet she had an early flight.

column5: Contraction: it's = it is | Possession: Maya's book, students' hall
column6: Use apostrophes to show omitted letters in contractions (don't, won't, let's) and noun possession. NEVER use an apostrophe to make regular nouns plural!
column7: Golden check: 'it's' ALWAYS means 'it is/it has'; possessive is 'its' (no apostrophe).
column8: It's a lovely day, and the dog is chasing its tail.||Who's coming to the writers' workshop tonight?||I can't find my brother's headphones.

column5: Semicolon (;) links two related sentences | Colon (:) introduces a list or explanation
column6: A semicolon joins two closely connected independent clauses without 'and/but' (or precedes '; however,'). A colon follows a complete sentence to introduce a list, quote, or explanation.
column7: Don't put a colon directly after 'such as' or a verb like 'are'.
column8: She didn't just read the rule; she practiced it ten times.||Bring three essentials: a notebook, a pen, and curiosity.||One habit changed everything: reading aloud every morning.

column5: She said, "Practice makes progress."
column6: Enclose exact spoken words in quotation marks. Start the quoted sentence with a capital letter and place commas/periods clearly around the dialogue tag.
column7: Do not use quotation marks around indirect reported speech.
column8: Could you repeat that slowly? asked the learner.||He smiled and replied, "Every mistake teaches you something."||My favorite proverb is "Slow and steady wins the race."

column5: Compound adj before noun: well-known author | Em dash (—) for dramatic pause
column6: Hyphenate two words acting together as a single adjective BEFORE a noun (a well-written essay), but usually omit the hyphen after the verb ('The essay is well written').
column7: Never hyphenate an -ly adverb + adjective ('a widely known fact', no hyphen).
column8: She is a well-known educator in our city.||We stayed at a family-friendly resort near the hills.||Only one thing mattered—keeping the streak alive.

column4: Its vs It's & Their vs There vs They're
column5: it's = it is | its = belonging to it | there = place | their = theirs | they're = they are
column6: The most frequent English homophone traps. Always mentally expand the contraction to test whether it fits the sentence!
column7: Test: replace 'they're' with 'they are'—if it breaks, pick 'their' or 'there'.
column8: They're parking their car over there near the gate.||It's clear that the puppy loves its new toy.||There is a quiet park behind their school.

column4: Affect vs Effect & Lose vs Loose
column5: affect (verb) vs effect (noun) | lose (verb: misplace) vs loose (adj: not tight)
column6: 'Affect' is almost always a verb (to influence); 'effect' is almost always a noun (a result). 'Lose' rhymes with 'choose'; 'loose' rhymes with 'goose'.
column7: Memory trick: RAVEN — Remember Affect Verb, Effect Noun!
column8: Lack of sleep directly affects your concentration.||Daily reading has a powerful effect on vocabulary.||Don't lose your passport — keep your pocket zip closed, not loose.

column4: Borrow vs Lend & Bring vs Take
