column5: borrow = receive temporarily | lend = give temporarily | bring = toward here | take = away
column6: 'Borrow FROM' someone; 'lend TO' someone. 'Bring' moves items toward the speaker/listener; 'take' moves items away to another place.
column7: Never say 'Can you borrow me a pen?' — say 'Can you lend me a pen?' or 'May I borrow a pen?'.
column8: Could you lend me your charger for an hour?||I borrowed three novels from the campus library.||Please bring your notebook when you come here tomorrow.

column4: Fewer vs Less & Much vs Many
column5: fewer + countable plural | less + uncountable singular
column6: Use 'fewer' for things you can count individually (fewer mistakes, fewer emails) and 'less' for bulk/uncountable nouns (less time, less noise, less money).
column7: Use 'less' with measurements of time, distance, and money: 'less than ten minutes'.
column8: You made fewer mistakes in today's quiz!||We spent less time waiting thanks to online booking.||Fewer people drove to work during the rainstorm.

column4: Say vs Tell vs Speak vs Talk
column5: say + words | tell + person | speak + language/formal | talk + to/about
column6: Each communication verb fills a distinct slot. We 'speak English', 'tell a story/the truth/a lie', 'say hello', and 'talk to a friend about plans'.
column7: Never say 'talk English' or 'say me the truth'—say 'speak English' and 'tell me the truth'.
column8: She speaks three languages effortlessly.||He told us a hilarious story about his trip.||Let's talk about your study plan after class.

column4: Lie vs Lay & Rise vs Raise
column5: lie–lay–lain (recline, no obj) vs lay–laid–laid (place sth, +obj)
column6: 'Lie' (recline) takes NO object; its past tense confusingly looks like 'lay'! 'Lay' (put down) ALWAYS takes an object. Same for 'rise' (no obj) vs 'raise' (object).
column7: 'I lay down for a nap yesterday' (past of lie) vs 'She laid the book on the table' (past of lay).
column8: I'm going to lie down for twenty minutes.||Please lay the folders neatly on the desk.||Yesterday he lay awake listening to the rain.

column4: Beside vs Besides & Hard vs Hardly
column5: beside = next to | besides = in addition to | hard = intensely | hardly = almost not
column6: Adding a single letter completely transforms these pairs! Don't confuse 'hardly' (almost none) with 'hard' (with great effort).
column7: 'He works hard' (diligent) vs 'He hardly works' (barely works at all!).
column8: She sat quietly beside the sunlit window.||Besides English, he is studying Japanese.||It was so foggy that we could hardly see the road.

column4: Sensible vs Sensitive & Historic vs Historical
column5: sensible = wise/practical | sensitive = easily affected | historic = famous | historical = about history
column6: False friends and near-twins confuse even advanced learners. Check the exact root meaning before using them in essays.
column7: 'A sensible decision' (smart) vs 'sensitive skin' (delicate).
column8: Wearing sturdy boots for the hike was a sensible choice.||She is very sensitive to constructive feedback.||Signing the peace treaty was a historic milestone.

column5: Use ONLY ONE negative word per clause
column6: Standard English uses a single negative: pair 'didn't' with 'anything/anyone/ever', OR use a positive verb with 'nothing/nobody/never'.
column7: Never write 'I don't know nothing'—say 'I don't know anything' or 'I know nothing'.
column8: I didn't see anyone in the hallway.||She has never missed a single rehearsal.||We can hardly wait for the results.

column5: Fix with: Period (.) | Semicolon (;) | Comma + FANBOYS | Subordinator
column6: Never mash two complete sentences together with no punctuation (run-on) or only a comma (comma splice). Choose one of the four clean connectors instead.
column7: Check every comma between two full Subject+Verb clauses!
column8: Wrong: I studied hard, I passed. → Right: I studied hard, so I passed.||Wrong: It rained we stayed in. → Right: Because it rained, we stayed in.||She loves poetry; her brother prefers science fiction.

column5: Place descriptive phrases directly beside the noun they describe
column6: When a sentence opens with an -ing or -ed phrase, the VERY FIRST noun after the comma MUST be the person or thing doing that action.
column7: Wrong: 'Walking to school, the rain soaked me.' (Rain isn't walking!) → 'Walking to school, I got soaked.'
column8: Walking through the market, we smelled fresh spices.||Covered in bright wildflowers, the meadow looked magical.||She served warm pastries to the guests on silver trays.

column5: Match forms in lists & pairs: reading, writing, and speaking
column6: Items joined by and, or, than, or correlative pairs must share the exact same grammatical form (all nouns, all -ing, or all infinitives).
column7: Parallelism makes essays and speeches sound crisp and memorable.
column8: She enjoys hiking, cycling, and swimming.||The course helps learners read faster, write clearly, and speak confidently.||Success depends not on luck, but on steady preparation.

column5: Verb/Adj → Noun phrase (decide → decision, grow rapidly → rapid growth)
column6: Turning verbs and adjectives into abstract nouns creates an objective, dense tone valued in academic papers and executive summaries—use moderately for clarity.
column7: Avoid over-nominalizing simple emails where active verbs read faster.
column8: The rapid expansion of cities increased housing demand.||Careful analysis of the data revealed a clear pattern.||Her timely intervention prevented a major delay.

column5: may, might, tend to, appears to, suggests that, is likely to
column6: Academic and professional writers avoid extreme absolute claims ('proves', 'always') and use hedging verbs/adverbs to state nuanced, evidence-based arguments.
column7: Top IELTS/TOEFL essays use cautious hedging naturally.
column8: Regular sleep tends to strengthen long-term memory.||The findings suggest that early exposure boosts pronunciation.||This policy is likely to reduce urban congestion over time.

column5: Replace repeated words with one/ones, do/did, so/not
column6: Native speakers avoid clunky repetition by substituting 'one/ones' for countable nouns, 'do/does/did' for verbs, and 'I think so / I hope not' for whole clauses.
column7: Use 'one' only for countable nouns, never uncountable ones.
column8: I lost my blue pen, so I bought a new one.||"Will the train be on time?" — "I hope so."||She plays tennis far better than I do.

column5: Informal: phrasal verbs, contractions | Formal: Latinate verbs, full forms
column6: Choose vocabulary and grammar to match your audience. Formal emails and essays avoid slang, contractions, and vague words ('a lot of', 'things', 'get').
column7: Compare 'get in touch' (friendly) vs 'contact us' (formal).
column8: Informal: Can you send me the info ASAP? → Formal: Could you please forward the details at your earliest convenience?||Informal: A lot of kids drop out. → Formal: Numerous students discontinue their studies.||Informal: We fixed the bug. → Formal: The technical issue has been resolved.

column5: Firstly, Turning to..., With regard to..., By contrast, In essence
column6: Signpost words guide your reader effortlessly through complex multi-paragraph arguments, showing how each paragraph connects to your thesis.
column7: Keep signposts varied and never force them into every single sentence.
column8: With regard to cost, solar energy has become remarkably affordable.||By contrast, rural commuters still rely heavily on private vehicles.||In essence, fluency grows from small daily conversations.

column5: Topic Sentence (main idea) + Supporting Details + Example + Mini-Summary
column6: Every strong English paragraph develops ONE focused central idea introduced clearly in its opening topic sentence and proved with concrete evidence.
column7: If a sentence doesn't support your topic sentence, move it to a new paragraph!
column8: Learning a second language sharpens cognitive flexibility.||For example, bilingual speakers often switch between tasks more smoothly.||Therefore, language study benefits learners well beyond travel.

column5: Active: clear & energetic | Passive: objective & process-focused
column6: Prefer active voice for emails, stories, and persuasive writing because it names who acts. Use passive deliberately in lab reports, processes, and tactful diplomacy.
column7: Active: 'The team solved the error.' vs Passive (tactful): 'An error was made in the invoice.'
column8: Our volunteers planted five hundred saplings along the riverbank.||Next, the coffee beans are roasted at 200 degrees.||Thank you—your request has been forwarded to the coordinator.

column5: in order to → to | due to the fact that → because | at this point in time → now
column6: Strong writers tighten bloated phrases without losing nuance. Trim redundant pairs ('basic fundamentals', 'past history') and empty openers.
column7: Shorter, sharper sentences dramatically improve readability and exam scores.
column8: Wordy: Due to the fact that it rained → Concise: Because it rained.||Wordy: At this point in time → Concise: Currently / Now.||Wordy: Make a decision about → Concise: Decide on.

column5: make a strong case | draw a conclusion | deeply concerned | highly likely
column6: Fluent English depends on natural word partnerships (collocations). Saying 'heavy rain' and 'strong coffee' sounds far more natural than 'big rain' or 'heavy coffee'.
column7: Learn adjective+noun and verb+noun collocations as single units.
column8: The research team reached a compelling conclusion.||Heavy rain caused severe delays across the region.||She made a persuasive argument during the panel.

column5: Base V1 (Open the book) | Neg: Don't + V1 | Polite: Please / Could you...
column6: Use the bare base verb without a subject to give instructions, recipes, warnings, or warm invitations. Soften imperatives with 'please', 'just', or 'could you'.
column7: 'Do' before an imperative adds polite warmth: 'Do come in!'
column8: Turn left at the traffic light and walk two blocks.||Don't forget to review your mistakes after each quiz.||Please take a seat while I fetch your file.

column5: What + (a/an) + adj + noun! | How + adj/adv (+ S + V)!
column6: Express sudden delight, surprise, or admiration. Remember 'What' needs a noun (and 'a/an' before singular countables); 'How' modifies a standalone adjective or adverb.
column7: Say 'What a beautiful day!' (with 'a'), NEVER 'What beautiful day!'.
column8: What a brilliant idea that is!||How quickly the semester passed!||What wonderful weather we're having today!

column5: prefer A to B | prefer V-ing to V-ing | would prefer to V1 | would rather V1 than V1
column6: Express general preferences with 'prefer (+ to)' and specific immediate choices with 'would prefer (+ to V1)' or 'would rather (+ bare V1)'.
column7: Pair 'prefer' with 'to' (prefer tea to coffee), NEVER 'prefer tea than coffee'.
column8: I prefer reading paper books to scrolling on screens.||Tonight I would prefer to cook at home.||She would rather cycle than sit in rush-hour traffic.

column4: Enough & Too with For + Person + To V1
column5: too + adj + for [person] + to V1 | adj + enough + for [person] + to V1
column6: Specify exactly WHO an adjective limit applies to using 'for + object pronoun + to + V1'. Never repeat the object pronoun at the end!
column7: Say 'The box is too heavy for me to lift', NEVER '...to lift it'.
column8: The explanation was clear enough for beginners to follow.||This suitcase is too heavy for her to carry alone.||Is the water warm enough for the kids to swim in?

column4: Be About To & Be On The Point Of
column5: be about to + V1 | be on the point of + V-ing
column6: Describe an action happening in the very next few seconds. Very vivid in narratives when combined with 'when + Past Simple'.
column7: Do not add a specific future time like 'next year' with 'about to'.
column8: Hurry up — the movie is about to start!||I was just about to leave when you knocked.||The scientist was on the point of giving up when she spotted the clue.

column4: Have Something Done vs Get Something Done
column5: have/get + object + V3
column6: Arrange for someone else to perform a task, or describe an unwanted experience happening to your property. 'Get' feels more informal or highlights effort.
column7: Notice the object sits strictly BETWEEN have/get and V3.
column8: We are having our kitchen repainted next week.||I finally got my broken screen fixed today.||She had her essay proofread before submission.

column4: What With, Given That & Seeing As
column5: Given that + clause | Seeing as + clause | Considering + noun/clause
column6: Introduce an obvious known fact as the foundation for a logical judgment or decision. Great for speaking fluency and persuasive writing.
column7: 'Given that' works seamlessly in formal essays and business briefings.
column8: Given that she only started last year, her progress is extraordinary.||Seeing as everyone is here, let's begin the workshop.||Considering the tight budget, the event looked magnificent.

column5: as if / as though + Past Simple (unreal now) or Past Perfect (unreal past)
column6: Describe how someone looks, sounds, or behaves by comparing it to an unreal scenario. Use present tense if the comparison might actually be true.
column7: 'He talks as if he knew everything' (he doesn't) vs 'It looks as if it's going to rain' (likely true).
column8: She ran as though her life depended on it.||He smiled as if nothing unusual had happened.||It feels as though spring has arrived early this year.

column5: whoever/whatever/whichever/however + clause
column6: Express 'no matter who/what/which/how' in concise, confident sentences. 'However + adjective/adverb' means 'no matter how...'.
column7: Remember 'However hard you try' (never 'However you try hard').
column8: However difficult the grammar looks at first, daily practice makes it clear.||Whoever finishes first can help check the answers.||Take whichever route avoids the downtown construction.

column4: Reflexive & Reciprocal: Each Other vs One Another
column5: each other / one another = mutual two-way action | themselves = self-directed
column6: Distinguish actions people do to themselves from mutual actions shared between people.
column7: Compare 'They looked at themselves' (in a mirror) vs 'They looked at each other' (eye contact).
column8: Good teammates always support each other during tough weeks.||The two friends hadn't seen each other since graduation.||They reminded themselves to stay calm before the speech.

column5: Being tired, he left early. | The storm hit, causing power outages.
column6: Opening with a present/perfect participle (-ing / having V3) states a cause smoothly; closing with ', V-ing' states an immediate result.
column7: Always verify the main subject matches the opening participle!
column8: Having completed all twelve tenses, she moved on to conditionals.||Not knowing the local dialect, he used friendly gestures.||He missed the early bus, forcing him to take a taxi.

column5: So + adj + be + Subject + that... | Such + be + noun + that...
column6: High-impact formal/literary inversion placing the intensity at the start of the sentence for dramatic storytelling or C1/C2 essays.
column7: Invert the auxiliary/be right after the fronted 'So + adj'.
column8: So compelling was her lecture that nobody checked their phone.||Such was the force of the wind that several signs fell.||So quickly did he adapt that colleagues thought he had lived there for years.

column4: Subjunctive & Formal Lest / Were It Not For
column5: Were it not for + noun | Had it not been for + noun
column6: Express 'without this crucial factor' in polished formal English. 'Were it not for' = present; 'Had it not been for' = past.
column7: Pair 'Were it not for' with 'would + V1', and 'Had it not been for' with 'would have + V3'.
column8: Were it not for her guidance, I would still struggle with tenses.||Had it not been for the alarm, we would have overslept.||Keep backup notes lest you forget key formulas before the exam.

column4: Determiner Phrases: Plenty Of, A Great Deal Of, A Couple Of
column5: a great deal of + uncountable | a number of + plural | plenty of + both
column6: Choose natural quantity expressions that match countable vs uncountable nouns accurately.
column7: Never say 'a great deal of students'—use 'a large number of students' or 'plenty of students'.
column8: She invested a great deal of effort into her pronunciation.||There is plenty of room for everyone in the hall.||We have a couple of minutes left before the quiz starts.

column4: Advanced Emphasis: Whatsoever, Indeed & By No Means
column5: not...whatsoever | by no means | indeed
column6: Add crisp rhetorical precision in formal arguments and reviews. 'By no means' means 'definitely not' (triggers inversion if placed first!).
column7: 'By no means is this easy'—note the auxiliary inversion!
column8: There was no evidence whatsoever to support the rumor.||Mastering grammar is by no means impossible with steady daily habits.||By no means should you memorize rules without speaking real sentences.
